name: Agreement with the Shoshone of September 26, 1872 (Brunot Agreement)
nations: Eastern Shoshone Tribe of the Wind River Reservation (Newe)
promises: The Shoshone ceded the part of the Wind River reservation set apart by the treaty of July 3, 1868 that lay south of a line along the Little Popo Agie and the North Fork of the Popo Agie (Article I, as quoted by the Commission).
The United States would spend $5,000 a year for five years for the use and benefit of the Shoshone.
The United States would pay Washakie, chief of the Shoshone, a salary of $500 a year for five years.

breaches.what: The Commission found the 700,642 acres ceded by this agreement (the Brunot lands) were worth eighty cents an acre, a total value of $560,513.60, on September 26, 1872, and that the $27,500 consideration, less than four cents an acre, was unconscionable. It entered an interlocutory order awarding the value of the lands less the $27,500 paid.

breaches.quote: purchase price of less than four cents per acre for lands worth twenty times that amount was shockingly low

landTaken: 700,642 acres of the 1868 reservation (Commission finding 3, Docket 63).
compensation: Under the agreement the United States spent $25,000 for the Shoshone and paid Washakie a salary totalling $2,500 (Commission finding 3). The Commission's interlocutory order of 1954 awarded the value of the lands at eighty cents an acre less the $27,500 paid. Final judgment and payment were not traced.
today: The Commission found the agreement was approved by an Act of Congress of December 15, 1874 (18 Stat. 291). Royce adds that the reserve had been within the country assigned to the Crow in 1851 and ceded by them in 1868, and cites acts of June 22 and December 15, 1874 confirming the agreement.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says Chief Washakie chose the Wind River Basin as its permanent homeland, but later agreements took the South Pass and Big Horn Hot Springs regions and allotment gave more to homesteaders, cutting the reservation from 4.4 million acres to about 2.2 million.

plain.promised: For ceding the southern part of the Wind River reservation, the United States would spend $5,000 a year for five years for the Shoshone and pay Chief Washakie $500 a year for five years.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1954 that the 700,642 acres ceded were worth $560,513.60, and that the $27,500 paid, less than four cents an acre, was unconscionable.
plain.today: The Commission's 1954 order awarded the land's value less the $27,500 paid. The final judgment and any payment have not been traced.
